findings.paper_title: River Cam, Chalk Streams and Tributaries – Strategic Review and Environmental Projects
findings.headline: Jesus Green Lock infrastructure repair costs exceed Conservators' resources; Council has discretionary power to fund but has not committed and has explicitly reserved liability position.
findings.detail: Council working with Conservators of the River Cam to understand Jesus Green Lock condition, engineering solutions and funding requirements. Navigation infrastructure costs exceed Conservators' resources from navigation income alone. Cambridge City Council Act 1985 s.12 gives Council discretionary (not mandatory) power to pay Conservators. Any contribution would require separate decision on purpose, benefits, affordability, risks and conditions. The 1985 Act removed Council's historic responsibility for Conservators' deficits. Conservators cannot be dissolved or have functions transferred by simple governance decision. Council's agreement to explore sustainable options is explicitly NOT acceptance of responsibility for Conservators' statutory functions, operational liabilities or future deficits.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors assess contingent liabilities. Jesus Green Lock is publicly visible failing infrastructure adjacent to Council-owned assets, creating potential pressure for council funding. Position is currently discretionary and uncommitted, but the issue is flagged as active and outcome uncertain.
findings.figures: No repair cost figures provided; no funding commitment made
findings.quote: Legal advice records that this is a discretionary power, rather than a statutory duty to fund the Conservators or make good any deficit. The 1985 Act removed the Council's historic responsibility to make up deficits incurred by the Conservators. Any proposal for a Council contribution would therefore require a separate decision under the Council's normal financial and governance arrangements, having regard to the purpose, benefits, affordability, risks and any conditions attached to the funding.

findings.paper_title: River Cam, Chalk Streams and Tributaries – Strategic Review and Environmental Projects
findings.headline: Council accepting up to £2.5 million in environmental grants with liabilities for maintenance, asset ownership and staffing yet to be defined.
findings.detail: Cabinet approving acceptance of up to £1.9m from Cambridge Water for chalk-stream restoration across Cambridge, and approximately £600,000 for Hobson's Brook pollution-mitigation scheme, forming complementary streams within Cambridge Chalk Stream Project (delivery July 2026–March 2029). No Council match funding currently assumed. However, final funding agreements must define eligible expenditure, Council staffing implications, procurement requirements, maintenance responsibilities, asset ownership, monitoring commitments, treatment of VAT, and arrangements if external funding or project outputs change. Agreements must not create material unfunded liabilities. Final terms not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: Large external grants enable environmental delivery without immediate council capital, but create future operational obligations. Finance directors must understand maintenance liability, staffing costs, and asset ownership after delivery completion. Agreements remain under negotiation.
findings.figures: Cambridge Water funding: up to £1.9 million; Hobson's Brook pollution-mitigation: approximately £600,000; total: up to £2.5 million; Council match funding: none currently assumed
findings.quote: Subject to confirmation of the final funding agreements, no Council match funding is currently assumed for CCSP. The agreements must nevertheless define eligible expenditure, Council staffing implications, procurement requirements, maintenance responsibilities, asset ownership, monitoring commitments, treatment of VAT and the arrangements applying if external funding or project outputs change.

findings.paper_title: River Cam, Chalk Streams and Tributaries – Strategic Review and Environmental Projects
findings.headline: Jesus Green river wall budget increased from £850,000 to up to £2,411,000 due to design changes revealed at detailed stage.
findings.detail: In October 2024, a budget of £850,000 was approved based on high-level assessment assuming conventional land-based construction. Subsequent arboricultural, engineering and geotechnical investigations revealed this was not achievable: the wall is actively moving and rotating; mature protected trees prevent land-based plant operation; water-based delivery methodology is required. The additional £1.56m reflects revised delivery method, specialist plant, and risk allowances. Two-stage competitive procurement planned with tender commencement by October 2026. Reliable cost estimate will be available for 2027/28 Budget Setting Report. Original budget already in MTFS; additional requirement requires council approval.
findings.matters: A major capital scheme has experienced 84% cost escalation between approval and detailed design stage, after site investigations contradicted original assumptions. Finance directors and lenders assess cost control and project delivery capability; this demonstrates significant design/site discovery risks materializing post-approval.
findings.figures: Original budget October 2024: £850,000; enhanced total project budget: up to £2,411,000; additional requirement: approximately £1.56 million
findings.quote: In October 2024, a budget of £850,000 was approved for repair works. That estimate was based on a high-level assessment of the length of wall requiring repair and assumed that conventional construction plant could operate from the bankside. Subsequent arboricultural, engineering and geotechnical investigations have demonstrated that this delivery assumption is not achievable... The enhanced total project budget estimate is up to £2,411,000.

findings.headline: Interest rate of 3.50% above gilt rate is higher than council's routine investment portfolio, reflecting credit risk
findings.detail: The development loans carry an interest rate of 3.50% above the 5-year treasury gilt rate on a quarterly variable basis, or approximately 2.70% above PWLB rates. This is explicitly stated as higher than rates the council earns on its remaining investment portfolio. The council describes this margin as reflecting the credit risk involved and providing protection against future interest rate movements.
findings.matters: The elevated rate compensates for credit risk but signals concentration of risky assets outside routine treasury management. Another finance director would recognize this as pricing an illiquid, unrated borrower at a premium reflecting genuine default risk.
findings.figures: 3.50% above 5-year treasury gilt rate (quarterly variable); approximately 2.70% above PWLB rates
findings.quote: The agreed interest rates receivable on the loans to CIP are higher than the rates that are currently being obtained on the remainder of the council's investment portfolio.

findings.headline: CIP cannot easily access alternative financing due to lack of credit rating and substantial security already pledged to council
findings.detail: The paper indicates that if the council declined to provide the additional £12 million, Cambridge Investment Partnership would face significant obstacles sourcing alternative financing. Any alternative funding would likely cost more because CIP lacks a formal independent credit rating and has already given substantial assets to the council as security against the existing £18.5 million loan facility. This effectively positions the council as CIP's only readily available lender.
findings.matters: Illustrates concentration of credit risk and borrower dependence. A lender would see a council as the sole financing source for an unrated borrower. Another finance director would recognize this as a binding constraint if the scheme requires further funding or if market conditions deteriorate.
findings.figures: CIP is a 50:50 joint venture; original facility £18.5 million with substantial security pledged
findings.quote: Seeking finance from an alternative provider – this may be challenging in the timescales required given the lack of formal credit rating and security over CIP assets already given to the council.

findings.headline: Build cost inflation and slower sales driven by Iran war force £12 million increase in development loan facilities mid-project
findings.detail: Cambridge is requesting to increase the maximum development loan amount to CIP by £12 million, raising total facilities from £18.5 million to £30.5 million. The increase is required due to external economic shocks: build cost inflation and slowing sales resulting from the Iran war have increased the project's cash financing requirement during the development phase. The council expects £11.1 million to be drawn in October-December 2026 alone, characterized as a 3-month delay in sales income. This requires an out-of-cycle decision in the current financial year.
findings.matters: Shows how external geopolitical shocks can rapidly increase a council's exposure to development schemes mid-project. A lender would see material and fast-growing exposure to a project now facing cost pressures. Another council's finance director would understand how quickly initial assumptions can be disrupted.
findings.figures: £12 million increase requested; facilities rising from £18.5 million to £30.5 million; £11.1 million planned expenditure between October and December 2026
findings.quote: The recent and ongoing war in Iran has meant that build cost inflation has increased and sales rates have slowed.

findings.headline: Depot Relocation project overspent by £1.272 million due to contractor delays and construction cost inflation.
findings.detail: The Depot Relocation programme to create an Operational Hub delivered an overspend of £1.272 million (actual £4.767 million vs budget £3.495 million). The report attributes this to delays from external contractors and notes the original capital bid was made five years ago, during which time construction cost inflation substantially increased the cost base.
findings.matters: This demonstrates how long-range capital planning is vulnerable to inflation and contractor performance risks, relevant to assessing delivery and cost management risks in other multi-year capital schemes.
findings.figures: £1.272 million overspend (actual £4.767 million vs budget £3.495 million)
findings.quote: It is important to note that the original capital bid was made over five years ago, and since then inflationary pressures—particularly in construction, materials, and labour, have significantly increased the cost base for delivery.

findings.headline: Business rates income fell £1.0 million short of budget due to ratings appeals resolved in year.
findings.detail: Business rates income underachieved by £1.0 million following a significant number of ratings appeals being resolved in year, representing concrete loss of revenue from a key income stream with ongoing volatility exposure.
findings.matters: This demonstrates volatility in a key council revenue source, with implications for budget stability and income forecasting reliability in future years.
findings.figures: £1.0 million underachievement
findings.quote: Underachievement of business rates income of £1.0 million following a significant number of ratings appeals being resolved in year.

findings.headline: Investment income £1.9 million above budget is temporary, driven by capital slippage and higher interest rates that will not persist.
findings.detail: The council achieved net investment income £1.9 million higher than budget due to higher cash balances from capital programme slippage throughout the year combined with sustained higher interest rates. The council explicitly states investment income will fall in future years as excess cash is deployed to fund the capital programme.
findings.matters: The favourable underspend is partly underpinned by one-off factors; the underlying structural financial position is less robust than headline figures suggest, weakening the sustainability of future budgets.
findings.figures: £1.9 million higher investment income
findings.quote: Investment income is projected to fall in future years as excess cash is applied to the council's planned capital programme.

findings.headline: Park Street Car Park redevelopment delivered £19.6 million under budget through strong contract management, reducing borrowing requirement.
findings.detail: The Park Street Car Park redevelopment opened fully in 2025-26 having spent £19.6 million less than its final budget of £32.797 million. The report attributes this to strong contract management. Since the project is funded from external borrowing, this underspend directly reduces the amount the council needed to borrow.
findings.matters: This demonstrates effective capital project delivery and cost control, reducing the council's borrowing requirement and ongoing debt servicing obligations.
findings.figures: £19.6 million underspend (actual £13.233 million vs budget £32.797 million)
findings.quote: The Council spent £19.6 million less than budgeted on the Park Street redevelopment, which opened fully this year, as a result of strong contract management. This project is funded from external borrowing, so the underspend reduces the need to borrow rather than releasing any new resource.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account overspend of £6.9 million driven by compliance costs forces £6.4 million cut to capital contributions, increasing borrowing requirement.
findings.detail: The HRA operating surplus was £6.9 million worse than budget, primarily driven by costs to comply with Awaab's Law (damp and mould repairs, £2.3m), interim fire safety measures including waking watch (£1.5m), void management (£1.5m), and rectification costs (£1.4m). To maintain minimum reserve levels, the council reduced its revenue contribution to capital by £6.4 million, forcing increased borrowing to fund housing investment.
findings.matters: This represents a structural deficit in HRA operations driven by ongoing regulatory requirements, forcing the council into increased borrowing for capital spending with implications for debt servicing costs and medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £6.9 million operating surplus shortfall; £6.4 million reduction in capital contributions; £2.3m, £1.5m, £1.5m, £1.4m for specific cost drivers
findings.quote: The impact of these overspends is that the revenue contribution towards HRA capital expenditure in year had to be reduced by £6.4 million in order to maintain revenue reserves above the target level. This will have a knock-on impact on future years, as it has increased the amount the council needed to borrow to fund its capital programme.

findings.headline: Jesus Green riverbank requires £1.561 million additional capital spending beyond existing £850,000 budget for urgent repairs.
findings.detail: The council has identified critical asset compliance pressures centred on the Jesus Green riverbank. Drainage engineering scoping works indicate costs will exceed the original budget. The council is dedicating its entire £1.930 million General Fund underspend into a new earmarked reserve to fund these additional costs, prioritizing Jesus Green with any surplus held for other asset compliance work.
findings.matters: This emerging capital liability has consumed the council's entire financial headroom for the year, reducing flexibility and indicating balance sheet stress on infrastructure maintenance.
findings.figures: £1.561 million additional costs on top of £850,000 already approved; £1.930 million underspend earmarked for this reserve
findings.quote: As such, it is proposed that the £1.930 million General Fund underspend be placed into an earmarked reserve, to fund first and foremost the additional costs associated with the Jesus Green riverbank (currently estimated at £1.561 million on top of the £850,000 budget already approved).

findings.headline: £1.767 million in planned revenue contributions to capital deferred to future years
findings.detail: Capital budget carry-forwards include £1.767 million that was planned as revenue-funded capital expenditure in 2025-26 but is now being carried to future years alongside associated General Fund carry-forwards.
findings.matters: Indicates capital schemes are not delivering to plan and affects how the council funds its capital programme from revenue; without Appendix D detail, the significance and reason for deferral are unclear.
findings.figures: £1.767 million
findings.quote: Approve the General Fund capital budget carry forwards listed at Appendix D, together with the carry forward of associated resources to finance this expenditure (including £1.767 million of planned revenue contributions to capital).

findings.headline: Council transfers full £1.930 million revenue underspend to new earmarked reserve for asset compliance
findings.detail: Cabinet approved creation of a dedicated earmarked reserve for asset compliance and transferred the entire 2025-26 General Fund underspend into it, rather than retaining underspend in general reserves. This signals asset compliance is the council's material priority.
findings.matters: Shows the council generated a significant underspend and has identified asset compliance as a specific, material funding pressure large enough to warrant a dedicated reserve.
findings.figures: £1.930 million
findings.quote: Approve the creation of a new earmarked reserve for asset compliance, and the transfer into this reserve of the net 2025/26 General Fund underspend of £1.930 million.

findings.paper_title: Development Loan to Cambridge Investment Partnership
findings.headline: Cambridge increasing its maximum loan exposure to Cambridge Investment Partnership by £12 million
findings.detail: Cabinet has unanimously recommended that Council approve an increase of £12 million to the maximum development loan amount drawable by Cambridge Investment Partnership LLP across three projects: Newbury Farm, ATS/Murketts Histon Rd, and Fanshawe Road. A corresponding increase to the counterparty limit in the Treasury Management Strategy is proposed.
findings.matters: Councils increasingly use development vehicles to fund infrastructure and housing; the size of lending to a single counterparty directly affects treasury risk and available cash resources, which peers and lenders monitor closely.
findings.figures: £12 million increase to maximum loan drawdown; £12 million increase to Treasury Management Strategy counterparty limit
findings.quote: Increase the maximum development loan amount to be drawn down by Cambridge Investment Partnership LLP in respect of Newbury Farm, ATS/Murketts Histon Rd, and Fanshawe Road, by £12 million. Approve a corresponding increase of £12 million to the total investment counter-party limit with CIP in the Treasury Management Strategy.

findings.headline: Rent regulation project ongoing through December 2026 to resolve tenant overcharging refunds
findings.detail: The council is working through refunds owed to tenants following prior overcharging of rents and service charges. The project will continue into at least December 2026 due to large number of refunds and account complexity. Both current and former tenant arrears are below target while this work proceeds. New software systems are being implemented to enable better account management.
findings.matters: This represents financial exposure from prior control failures and means tenant arrears figures remain distorted until project completion.
findings.figures: Ongoing through at least December 2026
findings.quote: Continued to work through the refunds owed to tenants following the overcharging of rents and service charges. Due to the large number of refunds and complexity of some accounts this work will be ongoing into at least December 2026.

findings.headline: Civic Quarter redevelopment decision in October creates budget uncertainty of £0.8m income loss
findings.detail: The council's budget contains contingent items dependent on Full Council approval of Civic Quarter redevelopment in October 2026. Corn Exchange venue closure from 1 January 2027 is forecast to create £0.662m income loss, with £0.154m Market Square project on hold pending decision. Should the project not proceed, significant income loss would still occur due to venue booking lead times.
findings.matters: Material budget uncertainty that could swing the council's financial position depending on a major capital project decision.
findings.figures: £0.662m Corn Exchange income loss; £0.154m Market Square; decision scheduled October 2026
findings.quote: The Communities Group is showing 0.7m of additional cost, which reflects the  loss of income from the closure of the Corn Exchange venue from 1st January 2027, as part of the Civic Quarter redevelopment project.  Should the project not be approved by Full Council in October, there would still be a significant loss of income  due to the lead-in times for booking acts.

findings.headline: Investment income outperforming budget by £0.329m due to higher interest rates lasting longer than expected
findings.detail: Council forecast investment income of £1.8m for 2026/27 against budget of £1.5m. The £0.329m outperformance reflects Bank of England base rate at 3.75% persisting longer than anticipated at budget setting. Higher cash balances from capital programme delays have also contributed to higher average investment balances available.
findings.matters: A positive offset to revenue pressures, showing the council is maximizing returns on cash reserves.
findings.figures: £1.8m forecast versus £1.5m budget; £0.329m outperformance; base rate 3.75%
findings.quote: Because interest rates have remained higher for longer than anticipated, we are expecting a higher income from investments.

findings.headline: £0.9m fire and damage costs plus £0.5m for Awaab's law damp compliance and £0.1m fire safety measures
findings.detail: The council is incurring significant unanticipated costs for fire damage (£0.9m) and building compliance. Increased housing repairs spending (£0.5m) is required to comply with Awaab's law on damp, condensation and mould, with sustained demand through winter. Interim fire safety measures including waking watch at properties cost £0.1m, reduced from 11 sites to 2 but continuing through January 2027.
findings.matters: These represent ongoing statutory compliance obligations driven by fire safety requirements and housing regulations that create continuing budget pressures not fully recoverable.
findings.figures: £0.9m fire damage; £0.5m Awaab's law compliance; £0.1m waking watch through January 2027
findings.quote: £0.9 million costs as a result of fire and other damage to properties, which could not be anticipated when budgets were set

findings.headline: £22.478m slippage on HRA capital programme delays housing delivery across multiple schemes
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme shows £22.478m of underspend with budgets requested to carry forward to future years. Major delays include Princess and Hanover (£7.573m, delayed by October 2026 CPO inquiry and planning complexity), Stanton House (£3.469m), Davy Road (£2.715m, planning submission delayed), and Ekin Road (£1.930m). These delays affect housing supply delivery targets.
findings.matters: Housing delivery is central to the council's capital strategy and debt sustainability. Major scheme delays affect planned revenue streams and statutory housing obligations.
findings.figures: £22.478m total slippage; £7.573m Princess and Hanover; £3.469m Stanton House; £2.715m Davy Road
findings.quote: Within 2026/27, there is an overall underspend on the HRA capital programme. As at Q1, budget totalling £22.478 million is anticipated to be requested to be carried forward into 2027/28 and subsequent years to allow projects to be completed.

findings.headline: HRA revenue deficit forecast £2.0m higher than budget, funded by reducing capital contribution and increasing borrowing
findings.detail: The HRA year-end operating deficit is forecast £2.0m higher than budgeted, mainly due to overspends on repairs and maintenance. To maintain reserves above target, the council plans to reduce revenue contribution to capital expenditure by £2.0m, increasing long-term borrowing requirements. Main drivers are £0.9m fire and property damage costs, £0.5m for housing repairs to comply with Awaab's law, £0.3m additional void costs, and £0.1m fire safety measures.
findings.matters: The council is shifting from revenue-funded to borrowed capital, materially increasing long-term debt and borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: £2.0m deficit; £0.9m fire damage; £0.5m Awaab's law compliance; £0.3m void costs; £0.1m fire safety
findings.quote: Based on data as at the end of June, the HRA's year end-operating deficit is forecast to be £2.0 million higher than budgeted, mainly due to overspends on repairs and maintenance. To ensure that the HRA balance can remain above its target level, the planned revenue contribution to capital expenditure for the year  may have to be  reduced by £ 2.0 million.

findings.paper_title: River Cam, Chalk Streams and Tributaries – Strategic Review and Environmental Projects
findings.headline: Council clarified it has no statutory duty to fund the Conservators of the River Cam or make good their deficits
findings.detail: Legal review confirms Section 12 of Cambridge City Council Act 1985 provides discretionary power to pay money to Conservators, not a statutory obligation. The 1985 Act specifically removed the Council's historic responsibility to make up deficits incurred by the Conservators. Any future Council contribution would require separate decision under normal financial and governance arrangements. Report emphasises this does not mean Council is accepting responsibility for Conservators' statutory functions, operational liabilities or future deficits.
findings.matters: Removes potential implicit financial liability for navigation infrastructure operated by separate entity; clarifies Council's discretion over any funding support
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Section 12 of the Cambridge City Council Act 1985 provides that the Council may, if it thinks fit, pay money to the Conservators. Legal advice records that this is a discretionary power, rather than a statutory duty to fund the Conservators or make good any deficit.

findings.paper_title: River Cam, Chalk Streams and Tributaries – Strategic Review and Environmental Projects
findings.headline: Council accepted up to £1.9 million in Cambridge Water grant funding for chalk stream restoration programme with no council match funding required
findings.detail: Cambridge Water (South Staffordshire Water) will provide WINEP (Water Industry National Environment Programme) funding to support Greater Cambridge Chalk Stream Project transition to city-wide programme. Funding covers development and delivery of restoration across chalk-stream network including Coldham's Brook, Cherry Hinton Brook, Hobson's Brook and Vicar's Brook. Additional approximately £600,000 to be secured for Hobson's Brook pollution-mitigation scheme subject to final funding terms agreement. Cambridge City Council is designated lead authority and accountable body. Delivery period July 2026 to March 2029. Funding agreements must clarify council staffing implications, procurement requirements, maintenance responsibilities, asset ownership, monitoring commitments and exit arrangements.
findings.matters: Significant external funding programme reduces council revenue exposure but creates delivery, procurement, maintenance and future liability obligations; council becomes accountable body for £1.9m+ capital programme; final funding terms still to be confirmed
findings.figures: Up to £1.9 million from Cambridge Water WINEP funding; approximately £600,000 for Hobson's Brook pollution mitigation
findings.quote: Approve the acceptance of grant funding of up to £1.9 million from South Staffordshire Water (Cambridge Water) to support the development and delivery of restoration projects across Cambridge's chalk-stream network

findings.paper_title: River Cam, Chalk Streams and Tributaries – Strategic Review and Environmental Projects
findings.headline: Jesus Green river wall capital budget increased from £850,000 to £2.441 million following discovery that original delivery assumptions were not achievable
findings.detail: Original budget of £850,000 approved October 2024 assumed conventional land-based construction plant could operate from the bankside. Subsequent site investigations revealed this would cause unacceptable impacts on mature trees' root-protection areas. Water-based delivery methodology with specialist plant required instead. Revised budget estimate now up to £2.441 million. Two-stage procurement process planned with cost certainty available for Budget Setting Report 2027/28. Failure to intervene creates risk of localised structural failure affecting Jesus Green Lido, Lock, foul-water pump-out facility, cycle routes and underground infrastructure.
findings.matters: Material increase in capital project scope (£1.6m+); funding source and timing for additional requirement not yet confirmed; delays or non-intervention create operational asset risk
findings.figures: £850,000 approved October 2024; revised budget up to £2.441 million
findings.quote: Recommend to Council to approve an increase in the Jesus Green river wall project budget from the £850,000 approved in October 2024 to a maximum of £2.441 million, to enable the stabilisation and replacement works to proceed

findings.headline: Loan drawdowns conditional on certified work-in-progress; loans secured against CIP assets
findings.detail: Additional loan amounts are subject to the same security and drawdown controls as the original £18.5 million facility. Drawdowns require certification by the council's employer's agent that capital work-in-progress has been incurred, and loans are secured against CIP assets. Drawdown is on a flexible basis, so actual amounts drawn may be less than the facility maximum if sales proceed faster.
findings.matters: Proper drawdown controls and security documentation mitigate credit risk in lending to a special-purpose development entity. This staged funding approach ensures capital is only advanced as development progresses and is essential to assessing the council's capital discipline.
findings.figures: £30.5 million total facility after increase; £11.4 million drawn to date
findings.quote: Loans are secured against the assets of CIP and can only be drawn down against capital work-in-progress as certified by the council's employer's agent.

findings.headline: Cambridge property market proves resilient with 20 units already sold or reserved despite cost pressures and slower sales
findings.detail: Despite the cost inflation and sales slowdown driving the additional financing request, the paper provides evidence that underlying demand remains sound. The Cambridge property market has proved resilient to past economic shocks including Covid-19 and interest rate rises. Twenty units have already been sold or reserved across the three schemes.
findings.matters: Demonstrates that property demand is holding up despite development headwinds, reducing the risk that the council's loans will become stranded or require restructuring as the projects progress.
findings.figures: 20 units sold or reserved across three schemes
findings.quote: There is strong evidence to suggest that the units remain ultimately highly saleable. The Cambridge property market has proved extremely resilient to past economic events, including Covid -19 and recent increases in interest rates. To date, across the three schemes, 20 units have already been sold or reserved.

findings.headline: Development loans generate interest income at 3.50% above gilt rates, with council receiving 50% of development profits
findings.detail: Loans advance at 3.50% above the 5-year treasury gilt rate on a quarterly variable basis, with this margin reflecting risk and providing protection against future rate movements. As joint venture partner, the council receives 50% of development profits generated by CIP. These returns flow to the council's General Fund.
findings.matters: Shows how the council deploys capital in a way that generates returns sufficient to offset costs and support service delivery. The variable rate structure protects the council if it needs to borrow funds to meet drawdowns.
findings.figures: 3.50% above 5-year treasury gilt rate, quarterly variable; 50% of CIP development profit to council
findings.quote: the interest rate which is set at 3.50% above the 5 -year treasury gilt rate on a quarterly variable basis. This provides sufficient margin to the council to reflect the risk involved  and provide some protection against future interest rate movements.

findings.headline: Build cost inflation and slower sales rates increase project's cash financing requirement, necessitating £12 million additional development facility
findings.detail: Cost inflation driven by external factors and slowed sales rates have increased the project's cash financing requirement during the development phase. The £12 million request is based on planned project expenditure of £11.1 million between October and December 2026 rounded up for contingency, and assumes a 3-month delay to sales income. £11.4 million of the original £18.5 million facility has already been drawn.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to understand whether major council capital commitments are delivering as planned. Cost overruns and demand slowdown indicate project headwinds that affect both cash flow and the returns the council receives from its 50% profit share.
findings.figures: £12 million increase; £11.1 million planned Oct-Dec expenditure; £11.4 million already drawn of £18.5 million facility
findings.quote: The recent and ongoing war in Iran has meant that build cost inflation has increased and sales rates have slowed. Acknowledging this, construction programming has be en reviewed and t he council's payments for the affordable housing has been reprofiled in line with new handover dates.

findings.paper_title: River Cam, Chalk Streams and Tributaries – Strategic Review and Environmental Projects
findings.headline: Jesus Green Lock structural concerns identified; Council exploring funding options under discretionary power
findings.detail: Jesus Green Lock requires structural intervention; costs recognised to exceed Conservators' normal resources from navigation income. Council working with Conservators to understand condition, costs and solutions. Section 12 of Cambridge City Council Act 1985 provides discretionary power to contribute (not mandatory duty). Paper notes legal requirement to separately assess affordability, benefits and risks of any contribution.
findings.matters: Identifies potential emerging liability affecting critical river infrastructure. Council's discretionary decision-making power indicates further financial decisions likely forthcoming. No committed funding yet, but material contingent liability depending on Conservators' eventual costs and Council's discretionary decision.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: Jesus Green Lock and Baits Bite Lock have required intervention because of structural concerns. A longer-term solution is required for Jesus Green Lock, and the Full Council motion recognises that the cost of major navigation infrastructure can exceed the resources normally available to the Conservators through navigation income alone

findings.paper_title: River Cam, Chalk Streams and Tributaries – Strategic Review and Environmental Projects
findings.headline: Officers approved to secure £600,000 for Hobson's Brook pollution-mitigation scheme, subject to final terms agreement
findings.detail: Nature-based pollution-mitigation scheme to intercept and mitigate pollution before reaching chalk-stream habitats. Second complementary element of Greater Cambridge Chalk Stream Project alongside Cambridge Water funding. Final value, funding conditions, approvals and ongoing Council liabilities must be confirmed before agreement completion.
findings.matters: Material funding commitment explicitly stated as subject to final terms agreement. Exposes Council to cost variation risk and undefined future liabilities until formal agreement signed.
findings.figures: approximately £600,000
findings.quote: Approve officers to secure grant funding of approximately £600,000, to develop and deliver a resilient, nature-based pollution-mitigation scheme for Hobson's Brook, subject to final agreement of the funding terms

findings.paper_title: River Cam, Chalk Streams and Tributaries – Strategic Review and Environmental Projects
findings.headline: Council approved £1.9 million grant from Cambridge Water for chalk-stream restoration across Cambridge
findings.detail: Funding agreement confirmed for Water Industry National Environment Programme (WINEP) allocation supporting Greater Cambridge Chalk Stream Project. Covers programme management, research, technical assurance and capital habitat delivery across Coldham's Brook, Cherry Hinton Brook, Hobson's Brook, Vicar's Brook and springheads (July 2026 to March 2029, with monitoring continuing). No Council match funding currently assumed.
findings.matters: Material external funding reduces Council's capital burden, but paper explicitly flags that agreements must define eligible expenditure, Council staffing implications, procurement requirements, maintenance responsibilities, asset ownership, monitoring commitments, VAT treatment and variation provisions. These liabilities remain undefined.
findings.figures: £1.9 million
